strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem (the diversity-quality trade-off induced by alignment) with a simple, lightweight, training-free method that requires no fine-tuning.

Very comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 datasets spanning short-form instruction following, real-world dialogue, and long-form creative writing; 11 diversity metrics x 2 quality metrics forming 22 bi-dimensional evaluation spaces; two novel aggregate indicators (Coverage/Dominance) grounded in multi-objective optimization concepts.

Thorough ablation studies: comparison of many routing strategies (logit-based, content-based, combined, random, LLM-judge), and a direct test of the core hypothesis via base-aligned vs. aligned-aligned collaboration (Table 4), which convincingly supports the necessity of using a less-aligned model for diversity.
Human evaluation (quality, diversity, creativity) complements automatic metrics and largely corroborates the automatic findings, adding credibility beyond metric-only claims.
Extension to discourse-level, long-form diversity metrics (turning-point and arousal diversity) is a thoughtful addition that automatic lexical/semantic metrics alone would miss.
Reasonably detailed appendix with formal metric derivations, reproducibility statement, and qualitative examples that make the paper largely reproducible in principle.
The efficiency argument (built on the superficial alignment hypothesis, sparse switching) is a nice practical property distinguishing this from costlier diversity-promoting inference-time methods.
weaknesses: Several qualitative examples in the appendix (e.g., Table A15) show clearly degenerate/gibberish outputs even from methods reported as high quality, raising concerns about how well the automatic quality metrics (perplexity, reward model score) truly capture failure modes, and whether aggregate numbers mask non-trivial fractions of broken generations.

The Coverage and Dominance indicators are custom-defined by the authors with normalization anchored to the same base/aligned model's own performance; this introduces a degree of self-referential evaluation design that could bias comparisons in the proposed method's favor, and is not independently validated against simpler, more standard evaluation protocols.

The method fundamentally depends on token-level compatibility (shared/aligned tokenization and word-boundary switching) between the two collaborating models, restricting applicability primarily to base/aligned pairs from the same model family; generalization to arbitrary model pairs or black-box APIs (aside from content-based routing) is not demonstrated.

The most 'principled' router variant, -JUDGE (using an LLM to make routing decisions), substantially underperforms simple heuristic routers, which is a somewhat concerning result suggesting the proposed heuristic routers might be closely tuned to the specific metrics being reported rather than reflecting a deeper principle of when diversity is beneficial.

Human evaluation is based on a modest sample (20 prompts x 2 datasets, 4 annotators, 3 outputs/method) and diversity/format judgments show only fair-to-moderate inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ = 0.166–0.268), limiting the strength of claims about human-perceived diversity gains.

The 'inherent early stopping' failure mode acknowledged in §6.2 could artificially inflate diversity metrics (shorter/incomplete generations may appear more 'distinct') without genuinely reflecting higher-quality diverse content, and its interaction with the reported quality metrics is not fully quantified.

Experiments are limited to two relatively small model families (Llama-3-8B, Olmo2-7B); it is unclear whether the reported gains persist at larger scales or for more heavily RLHF'd/safety-tuned models, where base-aligned divergence patterns may differ substantially.

The controllability claim (adjusting the routing threshold to move along the diversity-quality frontier) is empirically demonstrated via post-hoc sweeps, but the paper does not provide practical guidance or a data-driven mechanism for selecting the threshold for a new task/user preference without exhaustive re-evaluation.
